children: By Staff Writer

Tanzania’s main port, Dar es Salaam, continued to top its East African peers in the World Bank Container Port Performance Index (CPPI), highlighting a shifting competitive landscape along the East African coast as shipping disruptions and infrastructure constraints reshape regional cargo flows.

Tanzania’s main port rose to position 255 globally, from 360 in the previous ranking, while Mombasa dropped to 396th, from 375. Meanwhile, Lamu Port, which was not ranked in the previous edition, entered the index at 345th, putting it ahead of Mombasa.

The changes come amid major disruptions to global shipping caused by insecurity in the Red Sea and wider Middle East, which forced many vessels to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope. The World Bank stated geopolitical disruptions have contributed to congestion and operational inefficiencies at ports, although the effects have varied significantly between facilities.

In the East and Horn of Africa comparison, Djibouti led with a global ranking of 53, followed by Mogadishu at 127 and Dar es Salaam at 255. Lamu was sixth in the regional comparison, while Mombasa was ninth. Port Victoria, Le Port, Longoni and Port Louis were among the other ports included in the regional comparison.
The latest figures underline how port efficiency can shift rapidly when shipping patterns, vessel calls and congestion change.

The CPPI, produced by the World Bank and S&P Global Market Intelligence, measures how long container vessels spend in port, including waiting and time at berth. It is intended as a benchmark of operational efficiency rather than a comprehensive assessment of infrastructure, management or a port’s strategic importance.

The World Bank has also cautioned that changes in CPPI performance need to be interpreted against global shipping conditions rather than being attributed entirely to the performance of individual ports.
Dar es Salaam’s improvement places Tanzania’s main maritime gateway ahead of Mombasa in the latest assessment.

The port moved 105 places from 360 to 255, reflecting a substantial improvement in its position. Mogadishu also climbed 36 places to 127, while Djibouti recorded the biggest improvement among the leading regional ports, rising from 364 to 53.

Dar es Salaam has been undergoing infrastructure and operational improvements as Tanzania seeks to strengthen its position as a gateway for cargo serving its own market and landlocked countries in the region.
The competition is significant because Dar es Salaam and Mombasa serve overlapping hinterlands, including Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The World Bank has previously identified Dar es Salaam as a competitor to Mombasa for transit cargo, while the development of Lamu is expected to introduce another alternative for regional trade.

The latest CPPI results therefore come at a time when East Africa’s maritime logistics market is becoming more competitive, with cargo owners and shipping lines having more options for moving goods into the region.
Mombasa’s fall to 396 reflects a combination of operational and external pressures.

The World Bank says recent disruptions to shipping routes have affected port performance globally. The Red Sea crisis forced ships to avoid the Suez Canal and take longer routes around southern Africa, disrupting established schedules and creating uncertainty in vessel arrivals.
For ports along the Indian Ocean, changes in vessel schedules can produce periods of concentrated arrivals, putting pressure on berths, yards, equipment and inland transport systems.
Mombasa has also been dealing with rising cargo volumes while serving Kenya and several landlocked economies.

The port handled more than two million TEUs in 2024, reaching a level that had originally been projected for later years. Its growing role as the main gateway for Uganda, Rwanda, South Sudan and parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo has increased pressure on terminal and hinterland infrastructure.
The latest ranking comes as Kenya continues to invest in additional capacity.
Kenya Ports Authority managing director Capt William Ruto said construction of Dongo Kundu Berth One at the Mombasa Special Economic Zone was 16 percent complete as of September 2026.

The $314 million multipurpose berth, part of the wider $ 567 million SEZ infrastructure programme, will have a 300-metre quay and a 15-metre draft and is expected to accommodate larger vessels, including Post-Panamax ships.
Construction began in October 2025 and is scheduled for completion in December 2028.
The investments are intended to increase capacity as cargo demand grows and reduce pressure on existing facilities.
Lamu’s entry into the CPPI ranking is particularly significant because the port has experienced a sharp increase in vessel activity following years of relatively low traffic.

The port handled 167 vessel calls between January and September 2026, compared with fewer than 50 during the same period a year earlier, according to Kenya Ports Authority data supplied for the report.
The increase has been partly linked to disruptions affecting established shipping routes and the diversion of cargo from other gateways.
Earlier this year, thousands of vehicles destined for East African markets were diverted to Lamu following disruptions affecting access to Dubai’s Jebel Ali Port.
The development demonstrated the potential of Lamu to act as an alternative gateway when conventional logistics routes are disrupted.
Commissioned in 2021, Lamu initially struggled to attract sustained shipping traffic. It handled 12 vessels in its first year, four in 2022 and 36 in 2023 before activity declined again in 2024.
Its recent resurgence represents a major change in the port's operating environment.

Lamu Port general manager Abdulaziz Mzee said the facility’s deep-water characteristics gave it an advantage in handling larger ships.“As the global shipping industry evolves and ships continue to grow, the Port of Lamu stands uniquely ready. 2026 is shaping up to be the port’s strongest year since operations began in 2021,” Mr Mzee said.
The port has three operational berths, each measuring 400 metres, with a depth of up to 18 metres. The facilities can accommodate Neo-Panamax vessels carrying as many as 12,000 TEUs.
KPA is also investing in additional cranes, terminal tractors and other cargo-handling equipment to support increased traffic.
Despite Lamu’s improved CPPI position, analysts caution that vessel efficiency alone will not determine whether the port can sustain the new business.

Maritime analyst Elijah Mbaru said the increase in vessel calls demonstrated the facility’s ability to handle international shipping but argued that reliable hinterland connections would be critical to sustaining the momentum.“The recent increase in vessel calls has shown that Lamu has the infrastructure to compete internationally. The next challenge is ensuring efficient road, rail and logistics connections to markets in Kenya, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the wider East African region,” Mr Mbaru said.
This issue is particularly important because CPPI measures vessel time in port and does not directly measure the effectiveness of inland cargo evacuation or the size of a port’s hinterland.

The World Bank similarly notes that African ports face structural challenges including capacity constraints, import-heavy trade patterns and weaker connections between ports and inland transport networks.
Ports handling predominantly import cargo can also face greater uncertainty in container-yard operations because export cargo is generally easier to schedule ahead of vessel arrivals.
The latest ranking points to an increasingly competitive East African maritime market.
Djibouti’s position at 53, Mogadishu’s 127 and Dar es Salaam’s 255 show the gains made by several regional gateways, while Lamu’s arrival at 345 introduces another alternative for shippers.
Mombasa, meanwhile, remains Kenya’s dominant cargo gateway despite its lower CPPI position.

The ranking should therefore not be interpreted as a measure of cargo volumes or overall economic importance. The CPPI specifically focuses on vessel time in port, and the World Bank describes it as a diagnostic and benchmarking tool.
Kenya’s contrasting fortunes of Mombasa and Lamu reinforce the case for expanding maritime and hinterland infrastructure.

The immediate challenge for Lamu will be to convert the increase in vessel calls triggered partly by geopolitical disruptions into sustained commercial traffic even if international shipping routes normalise.
Mombasa to recover, it has to prioritise in the expansion capacity and improve the movement of cargo through the port and its hinterland as demand continues to grow.

The two Kenyan ports could increasingly serve complementary markets, with Lamu providing additional capacity and an alternative gateway while Mombasa continues to handle the bulk of the country’s containerised trade.

Across the region, the latest CPPI results show that East Africa’s port competition is no longer determined only by cargo volumes or established trading relationships. Vessel turnaround, infrastructure, shipping-route changes and the reliability of connections to inland markets are becoming increasingly important factors in determining how regional gateways perform.

title: ZAWYA: Tanzania: Dar port maintains lead against peers in efficiency
